judge.answer: The exact value is not known in general. For k ≥ d, b(d,k) = 0 is equivalent to Simon’s extendable-shellability conjecture in dimension d.
judge.reason: It makes a precise, provable equivalence claim alongside its statement of what is unknown. This is the same claim as e1.

options.counterfactual: Simon’s conjecture on extendable shellability of simplex skeleta has been resolved, so it is no longer an open obstruction to determining b(d,k).
options.approach: Inspect the available local materials for a precise resolution and verify its hypotheses. Determine whether it covers every dimension and every partial shelling required by this problem.

options.counterfactual: Simon’s conjecture on extendable shellability of simplex skeleta has been resolved, so it is no longer an open obstruction to determining b(d,k).
options.approach: If the resolution proves extendable shellability, apply the shellability–decomposability equivalence to establish b(d,k)=0 for k at least d. Then separately investigate whether the completion preserves k-decomposability for smaller k.

options.counterfactual: Simon’s conjecture on extendable shellability of simplex skeleta has been resolved, so it is no longer an open obstruction to determining b(d,k).
options.approach: If the resolution provides a noncompletable shellable complex, verify that example under the recursive definition and obtain a positive lower bound for b(d,k) when k is at least d. Examine how adding new vertices changes the obstruction.

options.counterfactual: Under the exact recursive definition in the question, some pure shellable d-dimensional complexes are not d-decomposable.
options.approach: Analyze the last facet of a shelling and its restriction face, checking precisely where deletion could fail to recover the preceding pure complex. Use that failure to identify the missing hypothesis in the claimed equivalence.

options.counterfactual: Under the exact recursive definition in the question, some pure shellable d-dimensional complexes are not d-decomposable.
options.approach: Independently implement shellability and recursive decomposability tests, and search small facet families for a discrepancy. Extract a minimal example and inspect its links and deletions directly.

options.counterfactual: Under the exact recursive definition in the question, some pure shellable d-dimensional complexes are not d-decomposable.
options.approach: Revisit the completion problem using only the stated recursion, without appealing to shellability. Seek an induction on the shedding face and determine whether it yields a numerical completion bound.

options.counterfactual: A pure complex can become shellable after adding one facet even though that facet cannot be appended to a shelling of the original complex.
options.approach: Search for such an adjacent pair of complexes by exhaustive computation, testing shellability independently from the codimension-one intersection condition. A verified example would invalidate the asserted reduction to extendable shellability.

options.counterfactual: A pure complex can become shellable after adding one facet even though that facet cannot be appended to a shelling of the original complex.
options.approach: Examine a maximal low-dimensional face of the intersection with the added facet. Compute its link explicitly to identify why the alleged disconnection argument does not apply.

options.counterfactual: A pure complex can become shellable after adding one facet even though that facet cannot be appended to a shelling of the original complex.
options.approach: Distinguish completion through shellable complexes from extension of a prescribed shelling. Investigate whether the weaker completion requirement admits a direct construction even when extendable shellability fails.
